item.content:encoded:
Long game theory rant:

+ show block
– hide block

1) The US didn't have perfect information when making their demand. The Foundation let them know of the information asymmetry through a transparent demonstration as a persuasive tactic. That's, like, a core tenet of game theory based policy.

2) This was set in '49, before people in the US even started thinking about concepts of mutual retaliation and deterrence and accepted a world with multiple nuclear powers. Game theory was barely a thing in academia at that point.

3) The idea that the nations act in a truly "rational" game-theoretic manner is purely hypothetical, and decidedly not true of individual humans. (Citation: The entire field of behavioral economics). Even if we assumed it were true, game theorists themselves point out that nations can act irrationally if they have incomplete/asymmetric information, which is always true.

We also can't treat nations as monolithic single decision-makers with no influence from individuals or emotions. For one relevant anecdote, the US under Carter and the following administrations (in addition to developing undetectable nuclear capabilities like SLBMs and openly telling the Soviets about them) decided that the best policy for deterrence and political pressure would be to tell the Soviets that the US would retaliate to a Soviet attack by blowing up the Soviet leadership first. In response, a Soviet political faction believed (pretty rationally) that the US would soon be capable to launch a first strike that they could not respond to, and thus advocated for an immediate Soviet first strike. In response to this faction, the USSR built the Dead Hand system, and (fun fact for the deterrence game theory equation), didn't tell the US about it.

Admittedly that doesn't have much to do with the story. If you found the implausibility outweighed the personal stories, that's a fair opinion, but the game theory isn't bent that far.

I didn't quite have the above reactions, mostly because Cold War intrigue doesn't interest me in fiction form, because no matter what's written about it in fiction, it will almost always be less insane than what happened during the actual Cold War. For instance, before the moon landing, the US's original plan was to detonate a nuke on the moon to blot out the sun for Russia.

Regardless, this was well-written enough to earn an upvote.
